title: Why Pet Insurance May Approve Cutting-Edge Treatments Before UnitedHealth Group
subtitle: The authors of a new study skipped right to accelerated TMS when it came to man's best friend.
body_html:
Ok, this is officially getting ridiculous. Depression—we have among the most remarkable treatments ever, already here, now, published, and more data are on the way. Those studies use transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, and accelerate it. If you need to learn more, my company, Radial, has a helpful explainer for you.

79% remission from depression with a 5-day treatment?1 Published. It’s called SAINT, and we offer it at Radial. 78% remission from depression with six half days? Top-lined. This paper uses the Brainsway H1 coil, and our group was the first to publish on this approach. The future is here, now, over and over again.

However, I’ll put a cash-money bet on your pets getting access to accelerated TMS before your family, at least it comes to UnitedHealth Group’s plans’ coverage.

Ok, Dr. Muir, what are you talking about? This paper cited a paper I’ve authored (thus generating an alert, which is why I’m aware of it):

Application of a novel three-day repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation protocol for the treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy in dogs: single-blinded randomised sham-controlled clinical trial

Now, transcranial magnetic stimulation has been studied in human epilepsy2 for a while. The evidence in human epilepsy is mixed:

For the current update, two of the eight studies analysed showed a statistically significant reduction in seizure rate from baseline (72% and 78.9% reduction of seizures per week from the baseline rate, respectively), whilst the other six studies showed no statistically significant difference in seizure frequency following rTMS treatment compared with controls (low‐certainty evidence).

However, our intrepid authors, publishing in Frontiers in Veterinary Medicine, with the help of leading human authors like yours truly, discovered a three-day protocol that demonstrated significant differences:

The monthly seizure frequency (MSF), monthly seizure day frequency (MSDF), and number of cluster seizures (CS) were recorded and comparisons between the two groups were analysed. The safety of the rTMS protocol was also evaluated. Statistically significant differences were identified between the groups in median MSF (active, 8 [0–24]; sham, 17 [7–46]; p = 0.04), MSDF (active, 8 [0–24]; sham, 11 [6–23]; p = 0.04), and number of CS (active, 10 [5–23]; sham, 16 [10–25]; p = 0.005).

And the TMS was well tolerated:

No adverse events were reported.

Though presumably, these were not first-hand reports from the research subjects. Although not listed in the supplemental materials, 100% of subjects were deemed to be “good boys” or “good girls,” and all were compensated with treats for participation, in keeping with the Westminster Declaration.

None of the subjects were lost to follow-up, as the protocol closely tracked whomsoever let the dogs out.

Ok, I’ll stop.

Now, to my bet…people love their pets. Oh, do they. And starting with pets is now a strategy among health-tech startups— lest we forget Theranos II? Or Loyal?

It’s also worth noting that Private Equity has been rolling up Veterinary Practices left and right:

In the depths of the pandemic, veterinary practices became unlikely targets of a deal-making frenzy fuelled by low borrowing costs. Sean Walter said he saw groups backed by private equity snap up veterinary practices at valuations of up to 30 times the clinics' annual earnings.

"If you talk to someone outside the veterinary industry," the Ottawa veterinarian and business consultant said of his conversations with others in the private-equity world, "and you tell them what some of these clinics have sold for ... their jaws drop."

And PE firms have been taking a swing at human TMS also…

First, private equity firms see high demand in this market. Behavioral health is desperately needed but is highly fragmented and lacking in innovation. Private equity is attracted to outpatient programs that target specific conditions that have evidence-based clinical models—programs aimed at addiction, eating disorders, and autism; these areas require less capital.3

As well as other major parts of human healthcare. With, truth be told, mixed results for their limited partners, patients, and physicians all.

However, despite the…ahem…profit motives being what they are, the dogs with intractable epilepsy space has a major upside from a deployment standpoint, when it comes to new, expensive, but effective technologies. They don’t have to put up with UnitedHealth Group and its prior authorization nightmares! UnitedHealth Group knows—I kid because I love. We are all on team healthcare, and given that United employs 10% of all American physicians, I have no choice but to work with them.

People spend an ungodly amount on their pets:

The number of insured pets is on the rise, and some platinum pet insurance, like Trupanion policies, covers treatments that humans can only dream of:

Our coverage includes a wide range of alternative and explorative treatments that go beyond traditional veterinary medicine. This comprehensive approach reflects the evolving nature of veterinary care, providing pet parents with more options when facing serious health challenges. Treatments covered for pets may include:

Bone marrow transplants — An advanced procedure primarily used for treating certain cancers and diseases affecting the bone marrow in pets, similar to human applications

Colloidal silver treatments — Used topically for its antimicrobial properties to treat infections and promote healing in wounds

Gold seed therapy — A form of brachytherapy used primarily in cancer treatment, involving the precise placement of small radioactive "seeds" to target tumors while minimizing damage to surrounding tissue

Herbal therapy — The use of plant-based remedies to treat various conditions

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy — Treatment that involves breathing pure oxygen in a pressurized chamber, which can accelerate wound healing and reduce inflammation

Kidney transplants — Complex surgical procedures are available for cats with end-stage renal failure, offering hope in otherwise terminal situations

Platelet rich plasma injections — A regenerative therapy that uses components from the pet's own blood to accelerate healing in tendons, ligaments, and other tissues

Polyethylene glycol medication — Often used in treating spinal cord injuries and other neurological conditions in pets

Stem cell therapy — An innovative treatment that utilizes the body's own regenerative cells to repair damaged tissue and treat conditions like arthritis

That is all covered by pet insurance.

I’m calling it now. Accelerated TMS for Dogs will be at scale before United covers it. Who’s taking the other side of the bet? I will be so, so thrilled to lose. Because right now…

And in those behavioral health guidelines…

I think Private Equity will see the goldmine in Accelerated TMS…except…for dogs. Cause despite ample evidence, United ain’t budging any time soon, when it comes to humans. United—I’m thrilled to be proven wrong. Call me! I promise, I’m a good boy— when you want to work collaboratively to get more access for more…people.
